![](images/Jupyter.png)

Welcome to your first hands-on session. You have already met **Positron** in your R course,
so the workspace itself will look familiar. Over the next hour you will learn what changes
when the language is Python, and you will build the first of the **Jupyter Notebooks** you
will write your code in for the rest of this course.

::: {.center-text .body-text-m}
Always remember: [**Python is the programming language. Positron is the IDE.**]{.teal-text}
:::

An *IDE* (integrated development environment) is a workspace that puts your code, its
output, your notes, and your files together in one place. Positron is the IDE we use.
Python is the language we write in it.

::: {.callout-note}
Positron runs both R and Python. The panes you learned in your R course, the Console, the
Variables pane, the Plots pane, and the file Explorer, all do the same jobs here. What
changes is the interpreter Positron is talking to, and the file format we write in.
:::

## Meet Positron on Posit Workbench

We run Positron on a shared **Posit Workbench** server, so there is nothing to install.
Everything happens in your browser.

#### Step 1: Log in to Posit Workbench

1. Open a browser and go to [workbench-1.bren.ucsb.edu](https://workbench-1.bren.ucsb.edu).
2. Enter your login credentials to access the server.

#### Step 2: Launch a Positron session

1. Click **+ New Session** and select **Positron Pro** from the list of session types.
2. If the dialog asks you to allocate resources, give the session at least **2.5 GB** of
   memory.
3. Click **Launch**. Workbench opens the session in your current browser window once the
   server has started it.

<!-- ![](images/positron_launch.png) -->

#### Step 3: Get your bearings

The Positron layout is the same one you used for R:

- The **Editor** in the center, where your notebooks and files open as tabs.
- The **Console** below or beside it, where Python evaluates code you type directly.
- The **Sidebar** on the left, holding the file **Explorer**.
- The **Session panes** on the right: **Variables**, **Plots**, and **Help**.
- The **interpreter dropdown** in the top right corner, showing which Python or R is
  currently running.

<!-- ![](images/interface-positron.png) -->

::: {.callout-note}
An IDE like Positron supports **interactive computing**: you run your code a piece at a
time and see each result immediately. That fast feedback loop is what makes it useful for
exploring data.
:::

#### Step 4: Point Positron at the course environment

Look at the interpreter dropdown in the top right. If it shows R, or shows a Python that is
not ours, click the ellipsis (`...`) next to it and choose **eds217_2026** from the list of
available interpreters.

:::{.callout-caution title="Switching interpreters clears your session"}
Changing the interpreter shuts down the old one and starts the new one, so any variables
you had defined are lost. Choose the right interpreter first, then start working.
:::

## Two ways to run Python

Positron can run your Python code in two places. It is worth seeing both once so you know
the difference.

### The Console (a REPL)

The Console is a Python prompt. This is a **REPL**, which stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop,
and it is the same idea as the R console you already use.

::: {.callout-note}
A **REPL** **R**eads what you type, **E**valuates it, **P**rints the result, and **L**oops
back for more. It is an interactive prompt for trying one line at a time.
:::

Click into the Console, type an expression, and press Enter:

```python
21 * 2
```

```
42
```

That is the whole read-eval-print idea: you typed an expression, it evaluated it, it
printed `42`. We are just watching the environment work here. You will learn Python's
syntax properly this afternoon, and its full set of operators on Day 3.

The Console is useful for quick checks, but nothing you type there is saved. That is why we
work in notebooks.

### Jupyter Notebooks (what we will use)

For the rest of this course you will write your code in **Jupyter Notebooks**, files ending
in `.ipynb`. A notebook lets you combine **code**, its **output**, and **narrative text** in
one document, so your analysis and the story of your analysis stay together. That is what we
want for data science, so notebooks are our home base from here on.

## Getting Started

Let's make the notebook you will use for this session. **We follow this same setup ritual at
the start of every session**, so it will quickly become second nature.

1. **Create a new notebook:**
   - Open the Command Palette with `Ctrl + Shift + P` (`Cmd + Shift + P` on macOS).
   - Type `New Jupyter Notebook` and select **Create: New Jupyter Notebook**.
   - A new, untitled notebook opens in the Editor.

2. **Save and name your notebook:**
   - Press `Ctrl + S` (`Cmd + S` on macOS) right away.
   - Name it with the format: `Session_1A_Positron.ipynb`
   - Saving immediately means you never lose work to a forgotten file name.

3. **Check the kernel:**
   - Look at the **Kernel Selector** in the notebook's action bar, along the top of the
     notebook.
   - It should read **eds217_2026**. If it does not, click it and choose that kernel.

:::{.callout-note title="Interpreter and kernel are two separate settings"}
The dropdown in the top right controls the Console. The Kernel Selector in the action bar
controls the notebook. Each notebook keeps its own kernel, so check it every time you open
a new one.
:::

4. **Add a title cell:**
   - Click the first cell and change its type to **Markdown**.
   - Add the following content (update the date to today):

```markdown
# Day 1: Session 1A - Positron & Jupyter Notebooks

[Session Webpage](https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/course-materials/interactive-sessions/1a_positron_notebooks.html)

Date: 08/31/2026
```

5. **Add a code cell** below the title cell. This is where you will start writing Python.

:::{.callout-caution}
Save your work frequently. Click the save icon or press `Ctrl + S` (`Cmd + S` on macOS).
:::

Throughout the session: take notes in Markdown cells, write and run code in Code cells, and
ask questions whenever you need to.

## Working with cells

A notebook is a stack of **cells**. Two kinds matter to us:

- **Code cells** for writing and running Python.
- **Markdown cells** for writing formatted text (notes, headings, links).

### Running a code cell

Click into your empty code cell, type the classic first line of code, and run it with
`Shift + Enter`:

```{python}
print("Hello, Positron!")
```

The output appears directly below the cell. `Shift + Enter` runs the cell and moves to the
next one. `Ctrl + Enter` (`Cmd + Enter`) runs it and stays put.

Watch the Console while you do this. Positron shows notebook execution there too, so the
Console and your notebook are working with the same Python session.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Change the message inside the quotes to greet yourself by name, then re-run the cell with
`Shift + Enter`. Did the output update?
:::

### Adding and moving cells

Hover between two cells, or below the last one, and Positron offers buttons to insert a new
**Code** cell or a new **Markdown** cell at that point. Each cell also carries its own small
toolbar for running, moving, and deleting it.

### Writing a Markdown cell

Add a new Markdown cell and try some formatting:

```markdown
## My notes

This is a **Markdown** cell. I can write:

- **Bold** with `**text**`
- *Italic* with `*text*`
- [Links](https://positron.posit.co/)
```

Run the Markdown cell (`Shift + Enter`) to **render** it into formatted text.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Add one more bullet to your Markdown cell, a link to the course website, then re-render it.
Try double-clicking the rendered cell to edit it again.
:::

## Handy Positron features

A few features that will save you time all week:

- **The Variables pane:** shows the names, types, and values of everything you have defined,
  and it updates as you run cells. This is the same pane you used to watch your R objects.
  It works for notebooks and the Console alike, with no extension to install.
- **The Data Explorer:** click a DataFrame in the Variables pane to open it as a sortable,
  filterable table. You will use this constantly from Day 4 onward.
- **Tab completion:** start typing a name and press `Tab` to auto-complete it or see
  suggestions.
- **Built-in help:** type `help(print)` in a code cell to read a function's documentation,
  or add a `?` after a name (`print?`) for a quick description. Pressing `F1` with your
  cursor on a name opens the same documentation in the **Help** pane.
- **Magic commands:** IPython adds special commands prefixed with `%`, like `%whos` to list
  your variables. You will meet these as needed.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
In a code cell, type `pri` and press `Tab`. Does Positron offer to complete it to `print`?
Then run `help(print)` and skim the description.
:::

:::{.callout-warning title="Limits of the Variables pane"}
The Variables pane is not the right tool for very large DataFrames or arrays. Use
`df.head()`, `df.info()`, and `df.describe()` for those, which you will learn on Day 4.
:::

## Saving and exporting

- **Save:** the save icon, or `Ctrl + S` / `Cmd + S`. Do this often.
- **Restart:** if your notebook stops behaving, use the restart icon in the action bar. This
  clears every variable, so re-run your cells from the top afterward.
- **Export:** Positron can render a notebook to other formats through Quarto. You will not
  need this until the final project, and we will cover it then.

## Key Points

- **Python is the language. Positron is the IDE** you run it in, hosted on Posit Workbench,
  so it is all in your browser.
- Positron runs Python in a **Console** (a read-eval-print prompt) or in **notebooks**, and
  we use notebooks from here on, because notebooks are saved and the Console is not.
- Set the **interpreter** in the top right for the Console, and the **kernel** in the action
  bar for each notebook. Both should read **eds217_2026**.
- A notebook combines **code cells**, their **output**, and **Markdown** narrative in one
  document.
- Run a cell with `Shift + Enter`. Use `Ctrl + Enter` to run without moving on.
- Start every session with the same ritual: **create, save with a name, check the kernel,
  title cell, save often.**
